params.title: SAFETY
params.subtitle: The FCC's RF exposure rules, then the lightning, tool, fire and electrical safety steps the exam asks about.

onScreen: RF exposure rules, then lightning, tool, fire and electrical safety
scenes.narration: This lesson is about staying safe around radio equipment. First, the rules of the FCC, the Federal Communications Commission, on RF, or radio frequency, exposure, and how RF and light can harm your eyes. Then the practical safety steps the exam asks about: lightning protection, using power tools, fighting an electrical fire, and preventing electrical shock. Let's begin with radiation exposure.

badges.label: Training and certification
badges.note: Anyone accessing an area where MPE power is present

scenes.narration: The FCC's exposure limits are called MPE, Maximum Permissible Exposure. Under FCC Part 1, in OET Bulletin 65 from the Office of Engineering and Technology, MPE compliance is averaged over time. In a controlled, or occupational, environment, exposure is averaged over 6 minutes. In an uncontrolled environment, where the general public may be, it's averaged over 30 minutes. And if MPE power is present, the personnel accessing the affected area must be trained and certified yearly.

params.title: When to evaluate RF exposure
items: Multiple-antenna sites: include every antenna above 5% of the MPE power density limit
An MPE study is required at an aggregate power level of 1000 watts ERP

onScreen: Include every antenna above 5% of the limit
MPE study at 1000 watts ERP aggregate
scenes.narration: Now, which transmitters count? At a site with multiple transmitting antennas, the RF site exposure evaluation must include every antenna producing more than 5 percent of the maximum permissible power density exposure limit. And an MPE study is required at an aggregate power level of 1000 watts E R P, that's effective radiated power. Aggregate means the total from all the transmitters added together.

params.title: How RF and light can harm the eyes
rows: Little blood flow carries heat away

onScreen: Portable radio RF: cataracts in the lens from heating
Live fiber: invisible infrared can burn the retina
Never look into a fiber optic cable
scenes.narration: RF can harm your eyes. Exposure from portable radio transceivers may be harmful because RF heating may cause cataracts. The eye's lens has little blood flow to carry the heat away. Light is a hazard too. Never look directly into a fiber optic cable. An active fiber signal may burn the retina, and because it's infrared light, you can't see it to know it's there.

callouts.label: A direct lightning hit: no device can protect the station
Surge protectors, grounding and bonding only limit the damage
Ground leads: sweeping bends; lightning jumps off sharp corners

onScreen: No protection from a direct hit
Grounding, bonding and surge protectors only limit damage
Ground leads: gradual, sweeping bends, no sharp corners
scenes.narration: Now the safety steps, starting with lightning. Is there a device that protects a station from a direct lightning hit? No. Good grounding, bonding and surge protectors can only limit the damage. How you run the ground leads matters too. Ground leads within a building should not have sharp corners. Lightning is not able to make sharp bends, so at a sharp corner it will jump off the ground lead. Use gradual, sweeping bends instead.

blocks.label: Shorted quarter-wave stub
blocks.note: Looks open at its tuned band

onScreen: Shorted quarter-wave stub: open at its tuned band
scenes.narration: A shorted-stub lightning protector is a quarter-wave stub on the feed line, shorted to ground. Do shorted-stub protectors work at all frequencies? No, only at the tuned frequency band. At that band, the quarter-wave stub looks like an open circuit to the signal, so the signal passes through to the radio, while lightning is shorted to ground. Away from its tuned band, the stub no longer looks open, so it can't be used at every frequency.

params.title: Power tools and electrical fires
items: Never use a power drill without eye protection
Chips, shavings and broken bits fly fast; keeping your face away won't stop them
Short-circuit fire: for the exam, choose the keyed answer FE30
Use a non-conducting agent: carbon dioxide, dry chemical or clean-agent gas
Never water or foam; de-energize the circuit if you can

onScreen: Power drill: always wear eye protection
Carbon dioxide, dry chemical or clean-agent gas
scenes.narration: Next, tools. You should never use a power drill without eye protection. Chips, shavings and broken bits fly at high speed, and just keeping your face away doesn't stop them. Now, fire. The exam asks what class of fire an electrical short circuit causes, and the preferred substance to put it out. The pool's choices don't really answer that, and electrical fires are actually Class C. For the exam, choose the keyed response, F E 30. In real life, a short-circuit fire involves energized equipment, so use a non-conducting agent: carbon dioxide, dry chemical or a clean-agent gas. Never water or foam, and de-energize the circuit if you can.

params.title: How a GFI socket prevents shock

scenes.narration: Last, the GFI, or ground fault interrupter, electrical socket. What is it used for? To prevent electrical shock. If current starts flowing along a ground path, perhaps through a person, the GFI senses that ground path current and shuts the circuit down. It trips at about 5 milliamps, a very small current. That's why GFI sockets protect people from dangerous shocks.
